note: columinibus = culminibus.

latin: ubi cerva silvicultrix, ubi aper nemorivagus?
english: where the forest-dwelling hind, where the grove-wandering boar?
note: No verb in the Latin.

latin: iam iam dolet quod egi, iam iamque paenitet.
english: now, now it pains me what I have done, now and now it repents me.
note: dolet, paenitet: impersonal verbs; 'me' supplied. iam iamque: 'now and now', i.e. now, even now.

audit.problem: The -que of iamque is omitted: the second pair is 'now and now', not 'now, now'.

latin: roseis ut huic labellis sonitus citus abiit
english: As from her rosy lips the swift sound went away,
note: huic: feminine dative, Attis.

latin: geminas deorum ad aures nova nuntia referens,
english: bearing new tidings to the twin ears of the gods,

latin: ibi iuncta iuga resoluens Cybele leonibus
english: then Cybele, loosening the yokes joined to the lions,
note: iuga: plural.

latin: laevumque pecoris hostem stimulans ita loquitur.
english: and goading the left-hand enemy of the flock, thus speaks.
note: laevum pecoris hostem: the lion on the left (the near one); "enemy of the flock" = lion.

audit.problem: The Latin ends with a full stop; the English changes it to a colon without a note.

latin: Agedum, inquit, age ferox i, fac ut hunc furor agitet,
english: Come, she says, come, fierce one, go, make frenzy drive this one,
note: No quotation marks added. hunc: masculine, Cybele speaks of Attis as male.

latin: fac uti furoris ictu reditum in nemora ferat,
english: make that by the stroke of frenzy he carries the return into the groves,

audit.problem: Possessive 'his' supplied with reditum without a note; not a forced function word.

latin: mea libere nimis qui fugere imperia cupit.
english: who too freely desires to flee my commands.
note: qui: masculine singular, Attis.

latin: age caede terga cauda, tua verbera patere,
english: Come, strike the back with the tail, endure your own lashes,

audit.problem: Possessive 'your' supplied with terga and cauda without a note; not a forced function word.

latin: fac cuncta mugienti fremitu loca retonent,
english: make all places re-thunder with bellowing roar,

latin: rutilam ferox torosa cervice quate iubam.
english: fierce, on the muscular neck shake the tawny mane.

audit.problem: Possessive 'your' supplied with cervice and iubam without a note; not a forced function word.

latin: ait haec minax Cybelle religatque iuga manu.
english: says these things threatening Cybelle and ties back the yokes with the hand.
note: religat: lit. "ties back"; here usually taken as "unfastens" the lion from the yoke. iuga: plural.

audit.problem: haec ('these things') is rendered 'Thus', iuga (plural, as the note itself says) becomes singular 'the yoke', and 'her' is supplied with manu.

latin: ferus ipse sese adhortans rabidum incitat animo,
english: The wild one himself, urging himself on, rouses himself raging in the spirit,
note: ferus: the lion. rabidum: masculine, predicative.

audit.problem: Possessive 'his' supplied with animo without a note; not a forced function word.

latin: vadit, fremit, refringit virgulta pede vago.
english: he goes, he roars, he breaks the thickets with wandering foot.

latin: at ubi umida albicantis loca litoris adiit
english: But when he approached the wet places of the whitening shore

latin: tenerumque vidit Attin prope marmora pelagi,
english: and saw tender Attis near the marble expanses of the sea,
note: marmora pelagi: "the marbles of the sea", i.e. its gleaming surface.

latin: facit impetum: ille demens fugit in nemora fera:
english: he makes an attack: that one, mad, flees into the wild groves:
note: ille: masculine, referring to Attis (some editors read illa).

latin: ibi semper omne vitae spatium famula fuit.
english: there always, the whole span of life, she was a slave-girl.
note: famula: feminine.

latin: dea magna, dea Cybelle, dea domina Dindymi,
english: Great goddess, goddess Cybelle, goddess, mistress of Dindymus,

latin: procul a mea tuus sit furor omnis, era, domo:
english: far from my house be all your frenzy, mistress:
note: sit: jussive subjunctive, "may it be". era: "mistress", Cybele.

latin: alios age incitatos, alios age rabidos.
english: others drive roused, others drive raving.
note: alios: masculine plural.

latin: Peliaco quondam prognatae vertice pinus
english: Once, sprung from the Pelian peak, pines
note: pinus (plural) = the timbers of the ship Argo, built from pines of Mount Pelion.

latin: dicuntur liquidas Neptuni nasse per undas
english: are said to have swum through the clear waves of Neptune
note: nasse = navisse, 'to have swum'; liquidas: 'clear, liquid'.

latin: Phasidos ad fluctus et fines Aeeteos,
english: to the floods of Phasis and the Aeetean bounds,
note: Phasis: river of Colchis; Aeetean = of Aeetes, king of Colchis.

latin: cum lecti iuvenes, Argivae robora pubis,
english: when chosen youths, the oak-strengths of the Argive young manhood,
note: robora: 'oaks, hard oak-wood', i.e. the strongest, the flower of the youth.

latin: auratam optantes Colchis avertere pellem
english: desiring to turn away from the Colchians the gilded fleece,
note: Colchis: dative/ablative of the Colchians; avertere = carry off.

latin: ausi sunt vada salsa cita decurrere puppi,
english: dared to run down the salt shallows with swift stern,
note: vada: 'shallows, waters'; puppi: 'stern', i.e. the ship.

latin: caerula verrentes abiegnis aequora palmis.
english: sweeping the dark-blue levels with fir-wood palms.
note: aequora: 'level surfaces', i.e. the sea; palmis: 'palms (of the hand)', i.e. the oar-blades.

latin: diva quibus retinens in summis urbibus arces
english: The goddess for whom, keeping the citadels in the topmost cities,
note: diva = Minerva, guardian of citadels; quibus is plural (the youths).

latin: ipsa levi fecit volitantem flamine currum,
english: herself made the chariot flying with light breath,
note: currum: 'chariot', i.e. the ship; flamine: 'blast, breath' of wind.

latin: pinea coniungens inflexae texta carinae.
english: joining the pine weavings of the bent keel.
note: texta: 'things woven', the joined planks.

latin: illa rudem cursu prima imbuit Amphitriten.
english: She first imbued with voyaging untried Amphitrite.
note: illa = the ship; Amphitrite (Greek accusative Amphitriten) = the sea; rudem: 'raw, untried'.

latin: quae simul ac rostro ventosum proscidit aequor
english: Which, as soon as with the beak it ploughed the windy level
note: quae: feminine singular, the ship; proscidit: 'ploughed up'; aequor: 'level', i.e. the sea.

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('with its beak').

latin: tortaque remigio spumis incanduit unda,
english: and the wave, twisted by the oarage, grew white with foam,

latin: emersere freti candenti e gurgite vultus
english: there emerged from the shining eddy of the strait, as to their faces,
note: vultus: accusative of respect ('as to their faces') with emersere; some take it as subject, 'faces emerged'.

latin: aequoreae monstrum Nereides admirantes.
english: the sea Nereids, marvelling at the portent.
note: monstrum: 'portent, marvel', i.e. the first ship.

latin: illa, siqua alia, viderunt luce marinas
english: On that light, if on any other, saw the marine
note: luce: 'light', i.e. day; marinas agrees with nymphas (line 17).

audit.problem: luce ('light', meaning day) is rendered 'day' in the English instead of kept literal with the meaning in the note, unlike lumine/lumina elsewhere.

latin: mortales oculis nudato corpore nymphas
english: mortals with eyes, with body bared, nymphs

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('with their eyes').

latin: nutricum tenus exstantes e gurgite cano.
english: standing out as far as the breasts from the white eddy.
note: nutricum tenus: 'as far as the nurses', i.e. the breasts (nutrix = nurse; by extension, breast).

latin: tum Thetidis Peleus incensus fertur amore,
english: Then Peleus is said to have been set on fire with love of Thetis,

latin: tum Thetis humanos non despexit hymenaeos,
english: then Thetis did not despise human marriage-songs,
note: hymenaeos: 'wedding-songs', i.e. marriage.

latin: tum Thetidi pater ipse iugandum Pelea sensit.
english: then the father himself perceived that Peleus was to be yoked to Thetis.
note: pater = Jupiter; iugandum: 'to be yoked', i.e. joined in marriage.

latin: o nimis optato saeclorum tempore nati
english: O you born in the too greatly longed-for time of the ages,

latin: heroes, salvete, deum genus, o bona matrum
english: heroes, hail, race of gods, O good of mothers
note: bona matrum goes with progenies (23b): 'O good offspring of mothers'.

latin: progenies, salvete iterum . . .
english: offspring, hail again . . .
note: Line 23b is preserved only in the Veronese scholia on Vergil; the rest of the line is lost and the dots are Merrill's gap marker, kept here.

latin: vos ego saepe meo, vos carmine compellabo,
english: you I often, you with my song shall I address,
note: meo goes with carmine: 'with my song'.

latin: teque adeo eximie taedis felicibus aucte
english: and you above all, exceedingly increased by fortunate torches,
note: taedis: 'pine torches', i.e. the wedding torches, the marriage; aucte: vocative, 'increased, enriched'.

latin: Thessaliae columen Peleu, cui Iuppiter ipse,
english: pillar of Thessaly, Peleus, to whom Jupiter himself,
note: columen: 'roof-ridge, pillar', i.e. mainstay.

latin: ipse suos divum genitor concessit amores.
english: himself the begetter of the gods, yielded his own loves.
note: Jupiter had himself loved Thetis.

latin: tene Thetis tenuit pulcherrirma Nereine?
english: Did Thetis hold you, the most beautiful daughter of Nereus?
note: Source misprint 'pulcherrirma' for pulcherrima, kept verbatim in latin. Nereine: 'daughter of Nereus'.

latin: tene suam Tethys concessit ducere neptem
english: Did Tethys grant you to lead her own granddaughter
note: ducere: 'to lead', i.e. to take as wife.

audit.problem: 'home' is added to ducere ('to lead'); the sense belongs in the note.

latin: Oceanusque, mari totum qui amplectitur orbem?
english: and Oceanus, who embraces the whole globe with sea?

latin: quae simul optatae finito tempore luces
english: Which longed-for lights, as soon as, the time being finished,
note: quae: feminine plural, referring to luces ('lights', i.e. days).

audit.problem: luces ('lights', meaning days) is rendered 'days' instead of kept literal with the meaning in the note.

latin: advenere, domum conventu tota frequentat
english: arrived, the house with gathering all throngs
note: tota (with Thessalia, line 33) is the subject: all Thessaly throngs the house.

latin: Thessalia, oppletur laetanti regia coetu:
english: Thessaly, the palace is filled with a rejoicing company:

latin: dona ferunt prae se, declarant gaudia vultu.
english: they bear gifts before them, they declare joys with the face.

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('with their face').

latin: deseritur Cieros, linquunt Phthiotica Tempe
english: Cieros is deserted, they leave Phthiotic Tempe
note: Cieros: town in Thessaly; Phthiotic: of Phthia.

latin: Crannonisque domos ac moenia Larisaea,
english: and the homes of Crannon and the Larisaean walls,

latin: Pharsalum coeunt, Pharsalia tecta frequentant.
english: they come together at Pharsalus, they throng the Pharsalian roofs.
note: tecta: 'roofs', i.e. houses.

latin: rura colit nemo, mollescunt colla iuvencis,
english: No one tills the fields, the necks grow soft for the bullocks,
note: The oxen are not yoked, so their necks lose the hardness of the yoke.

latin: non humilis curvis purgatur vinea rastris,
english: not is the low vine cleansed with curved rakes,

latin: non glaebam prono convellit vomere taurus,
english: not does the bull tear up the clod with down-sloping ploughshare,

latin: non falx attenuat frondatorum arboris umbram,
english: not does the sickle of the pruners thin the shade of the tree,

latin: squalida desertis robigo infertur aratris.
english: squalid rust is brought upon the deserted ploughs.

latin: ipsius at sedes, quacumque opulenta recessit
english: But his own abode, wherever the opulent receded
note: ipsius = of Peleus himself; recessit: 'withdrew', i.e. extended back into its inner rooms.

latin: regia, fulgenti splendent auro atque argento.
english: palace, gleams with shining gold and silver.
note: splendent is plural, agreeing with sedes.

latin: candet ebur soliis, conlucent pocula mensae,
english: Ivory gleams white on the thrones, cups shine together on the table,

latin: tota domus gaudet regali splendida gaza.
english: the whole house rejoices, splendid with royal treasure.

latin: pulvinar vero divae geniale locatur
english: The nuptial couch of the goddess, indeed, is placed
note: pulvinar: a cushioned couch (properly one for gods); geniale: of the marriage-bed.

latin: sedibus in mediis, Indo quod dente politum
english: in the middle of the abode, which, polished with Indian tooth,
note: dente: 'tooth', i.e. ivory; quod: neuter, the couch.

latin: tincta tegit roseo conchyli purpura fuco.
english: purple of the shellfish, dyed with rosy dye, covers.
note: conchyli purpura: the purple of the murex shell; the purple coverlet covers the couch.

latin: haec vestis priscis hominum variata figuris
english: This coverlet, varied with the ancient figures of men,
note: vestis: 'garment, cloth', here the embroidered coverlet.

latin: heroum mira virtutes indicat arte.
english: shows the virtues of heroes with wondrous art.

latin: namque fluentisono prospectans litore Diae
english: For, looking out from the wave-sounding shore of Dia,
note: Dia: the island (identified with Naxos) where Ariadna was left.

latin: Thesea cedentem celeri cum classe tuetur
english: she watches Theseus departing with swift fleet,

latin: indomitos in corde gerens Ariadna furores,
english: Ariadna, bearing untamed madnesses in the heart,
note: furores (plural): 'madnesses, frenzies'.

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('in her heart').

latin: necdum etiam sese quae visit visere credit,
english: and not yet even does she believe that she sees what she sees,

latin: ut pote fallaci quae tunc primum excita somno
english: inasmuch as she, then first roused from deceitful sleep,
note: ut pote ... quae: 'as being one who'.

latin: desertam in sola miseram se cernat harena.
english: sees herself, deserted, wretched, on the lonely sand.

latin: immemor at iuvenis fugiens pellit vada remis,
english: But the unmindful youth, fleeing, strikes the shallows with oars,
note: immemor: 'unmindful, forgetful'.

latin: irrita ventosae linquens promissa procellae.
english: leaving unfulfilled promises to the windy gale.

latin: quem procul ex alga maestis Minois ocellis
english: Him, far off, from the seaweed, with sad little eyes the daughter of Minos,
note: Minois: 'daughter of Minos' = Ariadna; alga: 'seaweed', i.e. the shore.

latin: saxea ut effigies bacchantis prospicit, eheu,
english: like a stone image of a bacchant, looks out at, alas,

latin: prospicit et magnis curarum fluctuat undis,
english: looks out at, and tosses on great waves of cares,

latin: non flavo retinens subtilem vertice mitram,
english: not keeping the fine headband on the yellow head,
note: mitram: the mitra, a headband or snood; vertice: 'crown, head'.

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('on her yellow head').

latin: non contecta levi velatum pectus amictu,
english: not covered, as to the veiled breast, with the light mantle,
note: pectus: accusative of respect; velatum (once veiled) is proleptic.

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('as to her veiled breast').

latin: non tereti strophio lactentis vincta papillas,
english: not bound, as to the milky breasts, with the smooth breast-band,
note: papillas: 'nipples, breasts'; strophio: a band worn round the breasts; tereti: 'rounded, smooth'.

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('as to her milky breasts').

latin: omnia quae toto delapsa e corpore passim
english: all which, slipped down from the whole body everywhere,

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('from her whole body').

latin: ipsius ante pedes fluctus salis adludebant.
english: before her very feet the waves of the salt were playing upon.
note: salis: 'of salt', i.e. of the sea.

latin: sic neque tum mitrae neque tum fluitantis amictus
english: So neither then for the headband nor then for the floating mantle's
note: vicem (line 69) governs the genitives: 'the plight of the headband ... of the mantle'.

latin: illa vicem curans toto ex te pectore, Theseu,
english: plight she caring, on you, from whole breast, Theseus,
note: ex te ... pendebat (line 70): 'hung on you'.

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('from her whole breast').

latin: toto animo, tota pendebat perdita mente.
english: with whole soul, with whole mind she was hanging, lost.
note: perdita: 'lost, ruined', i.e. desperately in love.

latin: ah misera, adsiduis quam luctibus exsternavit
english: Ah wretched girl, whom with unceasing griefs drove out of her mind
note: exsternavit: 'maddened, drove out of her senses'.

latin: spinosas Erycina serens in pectore curas
english: Erycina, sowing thorny cares in the breast,
note: Erycina = Venus of Eryx; pectore: Ariadna's breast.

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('in her breast').

latin: illa tempestate, ferox quo ex tempore Theseus
english: at that season, from which time fierce Theseus,

latin: egressus curvis e litoribus Piraei
english: having gone out from the curved shores of Piraeus,

latin: attigit iniusti regis Gortynia tecta.
english: reached the Gortynian roofs of the unjust king.
note: Gortynian = Cretan (Gortyn, a Cretan city); the king is Minos.

latin: nam perhibent olim crudeli peste coactam
english: For they relate that once, compelled by a cruel plague
note: coactam: feminine singular, agreeing with Cecropiam (line 79), i.e. Athens.

latin: Androgeoneae poenas exsolvere caedis
english: to pay the penalties of the Androgeonean slaughter,
note: Androgeos, son of Minos, killed at Athens.

latin: electos iuvenes simul et decus innuptarum
english: chosen youths and at the same time the pride of the unmarried girls

latin: Cecropiam solitam esse dapem dare Minotauro.
english: Cecropia was accustomed to give as a feast to the Minotaur.
note: Cecropia = Athens (from Cecrops); dapem: 'feast, banquet'.

latin: quis angusta malis cum moenia vexarentur,
english: With which ills when the narrow walls were vexed,
note: quis = quibus, referring to these ills; angusta: 'narrow, straitened'.

latin: ipse suum Theseus pro caris corpus Athenis
english: Theseus himself, for dear Athens, his own body

latin: proicere optavit potius quam talia Cretam
english: chose to cast forth rather than that such to Crete

latin: funera Cecropiae nec funera portarentur.
english: funerals of Cecropia, and not funerals, should be carried.
note: funera: 'funerals, corpses'; funera nec funera: living victims, dead and yet not dead.

latin: atque ita nave levi nitens ac lenibus auris
english: And so, striving with light ship and gentle breezes,

latin: magnanimum ad Minoa venit sedesque superbas.
english: he comes to great-souled Minos and the proud seats.
note: Minoa: Greek accusative of Minos.

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('and his proud seats').

latin: hunc simul ac cupido conspexit lumine virgo
english: Him, as soon as with desiring light the maiden looked upon,
note: lumine: 'light', i.e. eye.

audit.problem: conspexit stands in this line but its English 'looked on' has been moved to line 87, leaving this line without its verb.

latin: regia, quam suavis exspirans castus odores
english: royal, whom, breathing out sweet scents, the chaste
note: virgo regia (86-87) = the royal maiden, Ariadna; quam refers to her.

audit.problem: carries 'looked on' (conspexit), a word from line 86 that is not in this line.

latin: lectulus in molli complexu matris alebat,
english: little bed nourished in the soft embrace of the mother,

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('of her mother').

latin: quales Eurotae progignunt flumina myrtos
english: such as the streams of the Eurotas bring forth, myrtles,

latin: aurave distinctos educit verna colores,
english: or the spring breeze draws out, distinct colours,
note: distinctos colores: flowers of various colours.

latin: non prius ex illo flagrantia declinavit
english: not before from him did she turn away the burning

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('her burning').

latin: lumina quam cuncto concepit corpore flammam
english: lights than she conceived flame in all the body
note: lumina: 'lights', i.e. eyes.

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('in all her body').

latin: funditus atque imis exarsit tota medullis.
english: from the depths and blazed up wholly in the inmost marrows.

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('in her inmost marrows').

latin: heu misere exagitans immiti corde furores,
english: Alas, wretchedly stirring up madnesses with unkind heart,
note: Addressed to Cupid; misere: 'wretchedly, cruelly'.

latin: sancte puer, curis hominum qui gaudia misces,
english: holy boy, who mingle joys with the cares of men,

latin: quaeque regis Golgos quaeque Idalium frondosum,
english: and you who rule Golgi and who leafy Idalium,
note: Venus; Golgi and Idalium are Cypriot cult-places.

latin: qualibus incensam iactastis mente puellam
english: on what, inflamed in mind, have you tossed the girl
note: qualibus agrees with fluctibus (line 98): 'on what waves'.

latin: fluctibus in flavo saepe hospite suspirantem!
english: waves, often sighing for the yellow-haired guest!
note: flavo hospite: the fair-haired stranger, Theseus.

latin: quantos illa tulit languenti corde timores,
english: How great fears she bore with fainting heart,

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('in her fainting heart').

latin: quanto saepe magis fulgore expalluit auri,
english: by how much, often, more than the gleam of gold she grew pale,
note: quanto ... magis: 'by how much more', with expalluit: she often grew paler than the gleam of gold; fulgore auri: ablative of comparison.

audit.problem: 'by how much more often' attaches magis to saepe; magis goes with expalluit and fulgore auri (paler than the gleam of gold).

latin: cum saevum cupiens contra contendere monstrum
english: when, desiring to contend against the savage monster,

latin: aut mortem appeteret Theseus aut praemia laudis.
english: Theseus sought either death or the rewards of praise.

latin: non ingrata tamen frustra munuscula divis
english: Not unwelcome, yet in vain, little gifts to the gods
note: Her offerings pleased the gods, yet her vows (that he survive and stay) proved vain in the end.

latin: promittens tacito succendit vota labello.
english: promising, she kindled vows with silent little lip.
note: labello: diminutive of labrum, 'little lip'.

latin: nam velut in summo quatientem bracchia Tauro
english: For as, on topmost Taurus, shaking the arms,
note: Taurus: the mountain range; bracchia: 'arms', i.e. branches.

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('shaking its arms').

latin: quercum aut conigeram sudanti cortice pinum
english: an oak or a cone-bearing pine with sweating bark

latin: indomitus turbo contorquens flamine robur
english: an untamed whirlwind, twisting the trunk with blast,
note: robur: 'oak-wood, trunk'.

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('with its blast').

latin: eruit (illa procul radicitus exturbata
english: uproots (that, far off, driven out by the roots,

latin: prona cadit, † lateque cum eius obvia frangens),
english: falls prone, † and widely, of it, the things in its way breaking),
note: Line corrupt, obelus kept. The transmitted 'lateque cum eius obvia frangens' does not scan or construe; the common emendation 'late quaevis cumque obvia frangens' gives 'widely breaking whatever meets it'.

latin: sic domito saevum prostravit corpore Theseus
english: so, the body tamed, Theseus laid low the savage one
note: saevum: the savage beast, the Minotaur.

latin: Liber ut innuptae poteretur flore novercae,
english: so that free he might possess the flower of an unwedded stepmother,
note: Liber here is the adjective 'free', capitalised at line-start in the source; text doubtful (some editors read liber ut innuptae as Merrill, others emend). The father wants his son dead so that he may marry the young woman unhindered.

latin: ignaro mater substernens se impia nato
english: the mother, laying herself under the unknowing son, impious,

audit.problem: A possessive not in the Latin is supplied without a note ('under her unknowing son').

latin: impia non verita est divos scelerare parentes,
english: impious, did not fear to defile the parent gods,
note: divos parentes: the gods of the family, the ancestral spirits.

latin: omnia fanda nefanda malo permixta furore
english: all things speakable, unspeakable, mingled with evil madness,
note: fanda nefanda: 'right and wrong'.

latin: iustificam nobis mentem avertere deorum.
english: turned away from us the justice-making mind of the gods.
note: avertere = averterunt.

latin: quare nec talis dignantur visere coetus
english: Wherefore they do not deign to visit such gatherings,

latin: nec se contingi patiuntur lumine claro.
english: nor do they allow themselves to be touched by clear light.
note: lumine claro: the light of day.

latin: Etsi me adsiduo defectum cura dolore
english: Although me, worn out by unremitting grief, care
note: defectum: worn out, exhausted; cura is the subject of sevocat on the next line.

latin: sevocat a doctis, Ortale, virginibus,
english: calls away from the learned, Ortalus, virgins,
note: doctis virginibus: the learned maidens, i.e. the Muses. Ortalus = Hortalus (Q. Hortensius Hortalus).

latin: nec potis est dulcis Musarum expromere fetus
english: nor is able to bring forth the sweet offspring of the Muses
note: fetus: offspring, i.e. poems; the subject is mens on the next line.

latin: mens animi: tantis fluctuat ipsa malis,—
english: the mind of the spirit: amid such great evils it itself surges,—
note: mens animi: lit. 'the mind of the spirit', i.e. my mind. fluctuat: surges, heaves like the sea; i.e. the mind is in turmoil.

audit.problem: 'my' is added to 'mens animi' and 'like a wave' is added to fluctuat (noted, but not in the Latin).

latin: namque mei nuper Lethaeo gurgite fratris
english: for lately, in the Lethaean eddy, of my brother

latin: pallidulum manans adluit unda pedem,
english: the pale little foot the flowing wave washes,

latin: Troia Rhoeteo quem subter litore tellus
english: whom, beneath the Rhoetean shore, the Trojan earth
note: quem: masculine, the brother. Rhoeteum: a promontory near Troy.

latin: Ereptum nostris obterit ex oculis.
english: snatched from our eyes, crushes.
note: obterit: tramples, presses down on (the buried body).
Merrill marks a lost line; many editors supply 'adloquar, audiero nunquam tua facta loquentem' (shall I speak to you? I shall never hear you telling of your deeds).

latin: nunquam ego te vita frater amabilior
english: never shall I you, brother more lovable than life,

latin: adspiciam posthac: at certe semper amabo,
english: see hereafter: but surely always I will love,

latin: semper maesta tua carmina morte canam,
english: always sad songs, through your death, I shall sing,
note: tua morte: ablative of cause, because of (or over) your death.

latin: qualia sub densis ramorum concinit umbris
english: such as beneath the thick shadows of the branches sings
note: qualia: neuter plural, agreeing with carmina.

latin: Daulias absumpti fata gemens Ityli,—
english: the Daulian, lamenting the fates of destroyed Itylus,—
note: Daulias: the woman of Daulis (Procne), changed into the nightingale; Itylus: her son, whom she killed.

audit.problem: 'bird' is added: Daulias is 'the Daulian (woman)', Procne, as the writer's own note says.

latin: sed tamen in tantis maeroribus, Ortale, mitto
english: but nevertheless in such great sorrows, Ortalus, I send

latin: haec expressa tibi carmina Battiadae,
english: to you these songs of the Battiad, pressed out,
note: expressa: squeezed out, i.e. translated; Battiades: Callimachus (descendant of Battus).

latin: ne tua dicta vagis nequiquam credita ventis
english: lest your words, entrusted in vain to the wandering winds,

latin: effluxisse meo forte putes animo,
english: you perhaps think to have flowed out of my mind,
note: i.e. lest you perhaps think your words have flowed away from my mind.

latin: ut missum sponsi furtivo munere malum
english: as an apple, sent as the secret gift of a betrothed,

latin: procurrit casto virginis e gremio,
english: runs forth from the chaste lap of a maiden,

latin: quod miserae oblitae molli sub veste locatum,
english: which, for the wretched forgetful girl, placed under a soft garment,
note: quod: neuter, the apple. miserae oblitae: dative of disadvantage, the poor girl who has forgotten it (to her cost).

audit.problem: The dative miserae oblitae is rendered as an agent ('by'), and 'her' is added to 'soft garment'.

latin: dum adventu matris prosilit, excutitur;
english: while at the coming of her mother she leaps up, is shaken out;

latin: atque illud prono praeceps agitur decursu,
english: and it headlong is driven in a downward course,
note: illud: the apple.

latin: huic manat tristi conscius ore rubor.
english: on her flows, over her sad face, a knowing blush.
note: huic: dative, the girl. conscius: guilty, aware.

latin: Omnia qui magni dispexit lumina mundi,
english: He who discerned all the lights of the great universe,
note: The speaker is the lock of Berenice's hair (translated from Callimachus).

latin: qui stellarum ortus comperit atque obitus,
english: who found out the risings of the stars and their settings,

latin: flammeus ut rapidi solis nitor obscuretur,
english: how the flaming brightness of the swift sun is darkened,
note: i.e. eclipses.

latin: ut cedant certis sidera temporibus,
english: how the stars withdraw at fixed times,

latin: ut Triviam furtim sub Latmia saxa relegans
english: how, banishing Trivia secretly beneath the Latmian rocks,
note: Trivia: Diana, the moon; on Mount Latmus she visited Endymion.

latin: dulcis amor gyro devocet aerio,
english: sweet love calls her down from her airy circuit,

latin: idem me ille Conon caelesti in lumine vidit
english: that same Conon saw me in the heavenly light,
note: Conon: the court astronomer of Ptolemy III.

latin: e Bereniceo vertice caesariem
english: from Berenice's crown the hair
note: vertex: the top of the head. caesariem: a head of hair, here the lock.

audit.problem: caesariem is singular (the one lock, as quam in 9 shows) but is rendered as plural 'tresses'.

latin: fulgentem clare, quam cunctis illa deorum
english: shining brightly, which to all of the gods she,
note: quam: feminine singular, the lock (caesariem).

latin: levia protendens bracchia pollicita est,
english: stretching out her smooth arms, promised,

latin: qua rex tempestate novo auctus hymenaeo
english: at which time the king, increased by a new marriage,

latin: vastatum finis iuerat Assyrios,
english: had gone to lay waste the Assyrian territories,
note: vastatum: supine of purpose. finis: accusative plural, borders, lands.

latin: dulcia nocturnae portans vestigia rixae
english: carrying the sweet traces of a nocturnal struggle,
note: rixa: brawl; the wedding night.

latin: quam de virgineis gesserat exuviis.
english: which he had waged over the virgin spoils.
note: quam: feminine, the rixa. exuviae: stripped-off spoils, i.e. her virginity.

latin: estne novis nuptis odio Venus, atque parentum
english: Is Venus an object of hatred to new brides, and the parents'
note: odio: dative, for a hatred.

latin: frustrantur falsis gaudia lacrimulis
english: joys do they frustrate with false little tears,

latin: ubertim thalami quas intra limina fundunt?
english: which abundantly within the thresholds of the bedchamber they pour?
note: quas: feminine plural, the lacrimulae.

latin: non, ita me divi vera gemunt, iuerint.
english: Not, so may the gods help me, truly do they groan.
note: Order: non vera gemunt, ita me divi iuverint: they do not lament truly, so help me the gods. iuerint = iuverint.

latin: id mea me multis docuit regina querelis
english: That my queen taught me with many complaints,

latin: invisente novo proelia torva viro.
english: when her new husband was visiting grim battles.
note: ablative absolute.

latin: at tu non orbum luxti deserta cubile,
english: But you, deserted, did not mourn an orphaned bed,
note: Ironical: the lock anticipates that she will say her tears were not for the empty bed.

latin: sed fratris cari flebile discidium?
english: but the tearful separation of a dear brother?
note: frater: Ptolemy III, her husband, styled her brother (he was her cousin).

latin: quam penitus maestas exedit cura medullas!
english: How deeply care ate out your sad marrows!
note: medullae: marrow, the innermost self.

latin: ut tibi tunc toto pectore sollicitae
english: how for you then, anxious in all your breast,

latin: sensibus ereptis mens excidit! at te ego certe
english: with senses snatched away, the mind fell out! But you I surely
note: excidit: fell away, i.e. you lost your wits.

latin: cognoram a parva virgine magnanimam.
english: had known from a little maiden as great-souled.
note: a parva virgine: from (the time you were) a little girl.

latin: anne bonum oblita es facinus, quo regium adepta es
english: Or have you forgotten the good deed by which a royal you gained
note: facinus: deed (perhaps the killing of her suitor Demetrius).

latin: coniugium, quod non fortior ausit alis?
english: marriage, which not another, braver, would dare?
note: alis = alius. quod: neuter, the facinus.

latin: sed tum maesta virum mittens quae verba locuta es!
english: But then, sad, sending off your husband, what words you spoke!

latin: Iuppiter, ut tristi lumina saepe manu!
english: Jupiter, how often you rubbed your eyes with your hand!
note: tristi = trivisti, syncopated perfect of tero (you rubbed); it could also be read as the adjective 'sad', which leaves the line without a verb. Others read tersti (you wiped).

latin: quis te mutavit tantus deus? an quod amantes
english: What god so great changed you? Or is it that lovers

latin: non longe a caro corpore abesse volunt?
english: not far from the dear body wish to be away?
note: i.e. lovers do not wish to be far from the beloved body.

latin: atque ibi me cunctis pro dulci coniuge divis
english: And there me to all the gods, on behalf of your sweet husband,

latin: non sine taurino sanguine pollicita es,
english: not without the blood of bulls you promised,

latin: si reditum tetulisset. is haud in tempore longo
english: if he should have brought his return. He in a time not long
note: tetulisset = tulisset.

latin: captam Asiam Aegypti finibus addiderat.
english: had added captured Asia to the borders of Egypt.

latin: quis ego pro factis caelesti reddita coetu
english: For which deeds I, given back to the heavenly company,
note: quis = quibus. reddita: rendered, paid over.

latin: pristina vota novo munere dissolvo.
english: discharge the former vows with a new gift.

latin: invita, o regina, tuo de vertice cessi,
english: Unwilling, o queen, from your crown I departed,

latin: invita: adiuro teque tuumque caput:
english: unwilling: I swear by both you and your head:

latin: digna ferat quod si quis inaniter adiurarit:
english: may he bear what is deserved, if anyone by it has sworn in vain:
note: quod: by which, i.e. by your head, object of adiurarit.

latin: sed qui se ferro postulet esse parem?
english: but who would claim himself to be equal to iron?

latin: ille quoque eversus mons est quem maximum in oris
english: That mountain too was overturned, the greatest which in those regions
note: quem: masculine, the mountain (Athos).

latin: progenies Thiae clara supervehitur,
english: the bright offspring of Thia rides over,
note: progenies Thiae: the Sun, son of Theia.

latin: cum Medi peperere novum mare, cumque inventus
english: when the Medes brought forth a new sea, and when the youth
note: The source prints 'inventus' (found); read as iuventus (youth), the usual text. The new sea is Xerxes' canal through the Athos peninsula.

latin: per medium classi barbara navit Athon.
english: through the middle, with a fleet, the barbarian, sailed Athos.
note: barbara: with iuventus of the previous line.

latin: quid facient crines, cum ferro talia cedant?
english: What will locks of hair do, when such things yield to iron?

latin: Iuppiter, ut Chalybon omne genus pereat,
english: Jupiter, may the whole race of the Chalybes perish,
note: Chalybes: a people of the Black Sea famed as ironworkers.

latin: et qui principio sub terra quaerere venas
english: and he who at the beginning under the earth to seek veins

latin: institit ac ferri fingere duritiem!
english: set about, and to shape the hardness of iron!

latin: abiunctae paulo ante comae mea fata sorores
english: Of a lock severed a little before, my fate the sisters
note: abiunctae comae: genitive in apposition to mea, i.e. the fate of me, a lock just cut; sorores: the sister locks.

latin: lugebant, cum se Memnonis Aethiopis
english: were mourning, when himself, of Memnon the Ethiopian

latin: unigena impellens nutantibus aera pennis
english: the only-born brother, striking the air with nodding wings,
note: unigena: born of the same mother, i.e. Zephyrus, brother of Memnon.

latin: obtulit Arsinoes † elocridicos ales equus,
english: presented, the winged horse of Arsinoe † elocridicos,
note: Crux kept: † elocridicos is corrupt, usually emended to Locridos (of Locrian Arsinoe). se ... obtulit: presented himself.

latin: isque per aetherias me tollens avolat umbras
english: and he, lifting me, flies off through the airy shadows

latin: et Veneris casto conlocat in gremio.
english: and places me in the chaste lap of Venus.
note: me supplied from the previous line.

latin: ipsa suum Zephyritis eo famulum legarat,
english: The Zephyritis herself her servant thither had sent,
note: Zephyritis: Arsinoe deified as Aphrodite of Zephyrium.

latin: Graia Canopiis incola litoribus,
english: a Greek dweller on the Canopic shores,

latin: †hi dii ven ibi vario ne solum in lumine caeli
english: † hi dii ven ibi so that not only in the varied light of the sky
note: Crux kept: the opening words are corrupt (editors read e.g. 'hic liquidi' or 'inde Venus'); ne solum ... sed ... quoque: so that not only ... but also.

latin: ex Ariadneis aurea temporibus
english: the golden, from Ariadne's temples,
note: tempora: the temples of the head.

latin: fixa corona foret, sed nos quoque fulgeremus
english: crown should be fixed, but we too should shine,

latin: devotae flavi verticis exuviae,
english: the dedicated spoils of a golden head,
note: devotae: vowed, consecrated. flavi: yellow-haired.

latin: uvidulam a fletu cedentem ad temple deum me
english: me, moist from weeping, going to the temples of the gods,
note: The source prints 'temple', a misprint for templa (temples, or regions of the sky).

latin: sidus in antiquis diva novum posuit:
english: a new star among the ancient ones the goddess placed:

latin: Virginis et saevi contingens namque Leonis
english: for, touching of the Virgin and the fierce Lion

latin: lumina, Callisto iuncta Lycaoniae,
english: the lights, joined to Lycaonian Callisto,
note: Callisto: the Great Bear, daughter of Lycaon.

latin: vertor in occasum, tardum dux ante Booten,
english: I am turned toward the setting, leader before slow Bootes,

latin: qui vix sero alto mergitur Oceano.
english: who scarcely, late, is dipped in the deep Ocean.
note: qui: masculine, Bootes.

latin: sed quamquam me nocte premunt vestigia divum,
english: But although by night the footsteps of the gods press me,

latin: lux autem canae Tethyi restituit,
english: yet the daylight restores me to hoary Tethys,
note: me supplied from the previous line. Tethys: the sea.

latin: (pace tua fari hic liceat, Rhamnusia virgo:
english: (with your leave may it be allowed to speak here, Rhamnusian maiden:
note: Rhamnusia virgo: Nemesis, worshipped at Rhamnus.

latin: namque ego non ullo vera timore tegam,
english: for I will not by any fear cover true things,

latin: nec si me infestis discerpent sidera dictis,
english: not even if the stars tear me apart with hostile words,
note: nec si: nor if, not even if.

latin: condita quin veri pectoris evoluam)
english: but that I unroll the stored-up things of a truthful breast)
note: quin evoluam: but that I unroll, i.e. I will unfold (as a book roll) the secrets of my heart.

audit.problem: quin + subjunctive evoluam is turned into a gerund 'without unrolling', losing the finite subjunctive clause.

latin: non his tam laetor rebus quam me afore semper
english: Not in these things do I so much rejoice as, that I shall be away always,

latin: afore me a dominae vertice discrucior,
english: that I shall be away from my mistress's crown, I am tortured,
note: discrucior: I am racked, tormented.

latin: quicum ego, dum virgo quondam fuit, omnibus expers
english: with whom I, while once she was a virgin, devoid of all
note: quicum: with whom (the mistress, or her head).

latin: unguentis, una milia multa bibi.
english: perfumes, together drank many thousands.
note: Doubtful sense: as a maiden's lock it shared only plain oils, though many of them; text debated (expers / vilia).

latin: nunc vos optato quom iunxit lumine taeda,
english: Now you, when the torch has joined you with the longed-for light,
note: quom = cum, when. taeda: the wedding torch.

latin: non prius unanimis corpora coniugibus
english: not sooner to like-minded spouses your bodies

latin: tradite nudantes reiecta veste papillas,
english: hand over, baring your nipples with the garment thrown back,
note: papillae: nipples, breasts.

latin: quam iucunda mihi munera libet onyx,
english: than the onyx pours pleasing gifts to me,
note: libet: pours as a libation. onyx: an onyx perfume jar.

latin: vester onyx, casto colitis quae iura cubili.
english: your onyx, you who in a chaste bed keep the laws.
note: quae: feminine plural, you brides.

audit.problem: casto cubili is ablative ('in a chaste bed') but is rendered as a genitive 'of a chaste bed'.

latin: sed quae se impuro dedit adulterio,
english: But she who has given herself to impure adultery,
note: quae: feminine singular.

latin: illius ah mala dona levis bibat irrita pulvis:
english: her, ah, evil gifts let the light dust drink, worthless:
note: illius: genitive, her gifts. irrita: void, unaccepted.

latin: namque ego ab indignis praemia nulla peto.
english: for I from the unworthy seek no rewards.

latin: sed magis, o nuptae, semper concordia vestras,
english: But rather, o brides, always may concord your,

latin: semper amor sedes incolat adsiduus.
english: always may constant love dwell in, homes.
note: vestras (previous line) ... sedes: your homes.

latin: tu vero, regina, tuens cum sidera divam
english: And you, queen, when, gazing at the stars, the goddess

latin: placabis festis luminibus Venerem,
english: you shall appease with festal lights, Venus,
note: festis luminibus: with festal lights, i.e. on festival days.

audit.problem: placabis is future but is rendered as present 'you appease'.

latin: unguinis expertem non siris esse tuam me,
english: lacking ointment do not let me, your own, be,
note: siris = siveris.

latin: sed potius largis adfice muneribus.
english: but rather endow me with lavish gifts.
note: adfice: affect, endow; me supplied.

latin: sidera cur retinent? utinam coma regia fiam
english: Why do the stars hold me back? Would that I might become a royal lock:
note: Merrill's text; others read 'sidera corruerint utinam!' (would that the stars would fall). me supplied.

latin: proximus Hydrochoi fulgeret Oarion.
english: next to Hydrochoos would shine Oarion.
note: Hydrochoos: Aquarius; Oarion: Orion; i.e. the heavens would be thrown into confusion, since they are far apart.

audit.problem: fulgeret is imperfect subjunctive (would shine, consequence of the wish) but is rendered as a present jussive 'let ... shine'.

latin: O dulci iucunda viro, iucunda parenti,
english: O pleasing to a sweet husband, pleasing to a parent,
note: A dialogue between the poet and a house door.

latin: salve, teque bona Iuppiter auctet ope,
english: greetings, and may Jupiter increase you with good help,

latin: Ianua, quam Balbo dicunt servisse benigne
english: Door, which they say served Balbus kindly

latin: olim, cum sedes ipse senex tenuit,
english: once, when the old man himself held the house,

latin: quamque ferunt rursus voto servisse maligne,
english: and which they report in turn served the vow spitefully,
note: voto (Merrill); many editors read nato (the son). Sense uncertain.

latin: postquam es porrecto facta marita sene,
english: after, the old man laid out, you were made a married one,
note: porrecto sene: ablative absolute, the old man stretched out for burial; marita: married, i.e. the door of a married household.

latin: dic agedum nobis quare mutata feraris
english: tell us, come now, why, changed, you are said

latin: in dominum veterem deseruisse fidem.
english: toward your old master to have abandoned faith.

latin: non (ita Caecilio placeam, cui tradita nunc sum)
english: Not (so may I please Caecilius, to whom I am now handed over)
note: The door speaks.

latin: culpa mea est, quamquam dicitur esse mea,
english: the fault is mine, although it is said to be mine,

latin: nec peccatum a me quisquam pote dicere quicquam:
english: nor can anyone say any wrong done by me:
note: pote = potest.

latin: †verum istius populi ianua qui te facit!
english: † but the door of that people who makes you!
note: Crux: the line is corrupt; qui is masculine. General sense: the people blame the door for everything.

latin: qui, quacumque aliquid reperitur non bene factum,
english: who, wherever anything is found not well done,
note: qui: masculine plural, the people.

latin: ad me omnes clamant, Ianua, culpa tua est.
english: at me all shout, Door, the fault is yours.
note: The shout is direct speech; no quotation marks added.

latin: non istuc satis est uno te dicere verbo,
english: Not enough is that, for you to say it in one word,

latin: sed facere ut quivis sentiat et videat.
english: but to make it so that anyone may perceive and see.

latin: qui possum? nemo quaerit nec scire laborat.
english: How can I? No one asks nor takes pains to know.

latin: nos volumus; nobis dicere ne dubita.
english: We want to; to us do not hesitate to say.

latin: primum igitur, virgo quod fertur tradita nobis,
english: First, then, that a virgin she is said to have been handed over to us,

latin: falsum est. non illam vir prior attigerit,
english: is false. Not her would her former husband have touched,
note: attigerit: perfect subjunctive, could have touched.

latin: languidior tenera cui pendens sicula beta
english: whose little dagger, hanging limper than a tender beet,
note: sicula: little dagger, i.e. his penis. cui: dative, whose.

latin: nunquam se mediam sustulit ad tunicam:
english: never raised itself to the middle of his tunic:
note: i.e. never got erect.

latin: sed pater illius gnati violasse cubile
english: but the father of that son to have violated the bed

latin: dicitur et miseram conscelerasse domum,
english: is said, and to have polluted with crime the wretched house,

latin: sive quod impia mens caeco flagrabat amore,
english: whether because his impious mind burned with blind love,

latin: seu quod iners sterili semine natus erat
english: or because the son was impotent, with sterile seed,
note: iners: sluggish, impotent.

latin: et quaerendus is unde foret nervosius illud
english: and one was to be sought from whom might come that more sinewy thing
note: nervosius illud: that more vigorous member, i.e. a potent penis.

latin: quod posset zonam solvere virgineam.
english: which could untie the virgin girdle.

latin: egregium narras mira pietate parentem,
english: An excellent parent you tell of, with marvellous devotion,
note: ironic.

latin: qui ipse sui gnati minxerit in gremium.
english: who himself pissed into his own son's lap.
note: minxerit: urinated, i.e. ejaculated; gremium: lap, i.e. into the son's wife.

latin: atqui non solum hoc se dicit cognitum habere
english: And yet not only this does it say it has known,
note: Subject: Brixia, next line.

latin: Brixia † chinea suppositum specula,
english: Brixia, set beneath the † chinea watchtower,
note: Crux: chinea is corrupt (editors read Cycnea, the Cycnean citadel).

latin: flavus quam molli praecurrit flumine Mella,
english: which the yellow Mella flows past with gentle stream,
note: quam: feminine, Brixia.

latin: Brixia, Veronae mater amata meae,
english: Brixia, beloved mother of my Verona,

latin: sed de Postumio et Corneli narrat amore,
english: but of Postumius and of Cornelius it tells the love,

latin: cum quibus illa malum fecit adulterium.
english: with whom she committed wicked adultery.

latin: dixerit hic aliquis, quid? tu istaec, Ianua, nosti,
english: Here someone may say, What? you, Door, know these things,
note: Direct speech; no quotation marks added.

latin: cui nunquam domini limine abesse licet,
english: to whom it is never allowed to be absent from the master's threshold,

latin: nec populum auscultare, sed hic suffixa tigillo
english: nor to listen to the people, but fixed here to a little beam
note: tigillum: little beam (the lintel).

latin: tantum operire soles aut aperire domum?
english: you are accustomed only to shut or to open the house?

latin: saepe illam audivi furtiva voce loquentem
english: Often I heard her with stealthy voice speaking,

latin: solam cum ancillis haec sua flagitia,
english: alone with her maids, of these outrages of hers,
note: flagitia: disgraceful acts.

latin: nomine dicentem quos diximus, ut pote quae mi
english: saying by name those whom we have mentioned, inasmuch as she to me
note: ut pote quae: as one who.

latin: speraret nec linguam esse nec auriculam.
english: hoped there was neither tongue nor little ear.

latin: praeterea addebat quendam, quem dicere nolo
english: Besides she added a certain man, whom I do not wish to say

latin: nomine ne tollat rubra supercilia.
english: by name, lest he raise his red eyebrows.

latin: longus homo est, magnas cui lites intulit olim
english: He is a long man, on whom great lawsuits once brought

latin: falsum mendaci ventre puerperium.
english: a false childbirth from a lying belly.
note: i.e. a feigned pregnancy.

latin: Quod mihi fortuna casuque oppressus acerbo
english: That to me, crushed by fortune and bitter mischance,
note: Addressed to Manlius.

latin: conscriptum hoc lacrimis mittis epistolium,
english: you send this little letter written with tears,

latin: naufragum ut eiectum spumantibus aequoris undis
english: that, shipwrecked, cast out by the foaming waves of the sea,
note: naufragum: object, you as the shipwrecked one.

latin: sublevem et a mortis limine restituam,
english: I may raise you up and restore you from the threshold of death,

latin: quem neque sancta Venus molli requiescere somno
english: whom neither holy Venus to rest in soft sleep,

latin: desertum in lecto caelibe perpetitur,
english: deserted in a celibate bed, allows,
note: caelebs: unmarried, solitary.

latin: nec veterum dulci scriptorum carmine musae
english: nor do the muses with the sweet song of old writers

latin: oblectant, cum mens anxia pervigilat,
english: delight, when your anxious mind keeps watch all night,

latin: id gratum est mihi, me quoniam tibi dicis amicum
english: that is pleasing to me, since you call me a friend to you

latin: muneraque et Musarum hinc petis et Veneris.
english: and seek from here gifts both of the Muses and of Venus.

latin: sed tibi ne mea sint ignota incommoda, Manli,
english: But lest to you my troubles be unknown, Manlius,

latin: neu me odisse putes hospitis officium,
english: and lest you think that I hate the duty of a host,
note: hospes: host, guest-friend.

latin: accipe quis merser fortunae fluctibus ipse,
english: learn in what waves of fortune I myself am sunk,
note: quis = quibus.

latin: ne amplius a misero dona beata petas.
english: lest further from a wretched man you seek happy gifts.

latin: tempore quo primum vestis mihi tradita pura est,
english: At the time when first the pure garment was handed to me,
note: vestis pura: the plain toga of manhood.

latin: iucundum cum aetas florida ver ageret,
english: when my flowering age was passing its pleasant spring,

latin: multa satis lusi; non est dea nescia nostri
english: I played many things enough; not is the goddess unknowing of us
note: lusi: played, i.e. love and light verse. dea: Venus.

latin: quae dulcem curis miscet amaritiem:
english: who mixes sweet bitterness with cares:

latin: sed totum hoc studium luctu fraterna mihi mors
english: but all this pursuit, through grief, a brother's death from me

latin: abstulit. o misero frater adempte mihi,
english: took away. O brother taken from wretched me,

latin: tu mea tu moriens fregisti commoda, frater,
english: you, you dying, broke my comforts, brother,

latin: tecum una tota est nostra sepulta domus,
english: together with you all our house is buried,

latin: omnia tecum una perierunt gaudia nostra,
english: all together with you have perished our joys,

latin: quae tuus in vita dulcis alebat amor.
english: which your sweet love in life nourished.
note: quae: neuter plural, gaudia.

latin: cuius ego interitu tota de mente fugavi
english: At whose death I from all my mind have banished
note: cuius: the brother's.

latin: haec studia atque omnes delicias animi.
english: these pursuits and all delights of the spirit.

latin: quare, quod scribis Veronae turpe Catullo
english: Therefore, as for what you write, that at Verona shameful for Catullus

latin: esse quod hic quisquis de meliore nota
english: it is, because here whoever is of the better mark
note: nota: mark, class. hic: here, i.e. at Rome.

latin: frigida deserto tepefactet membra cubili,
english: warms his cold limbs in the deserted bed,
note: i.e. the bed Catullus has left.

latin: id, Manli, non est turpe, magis miserum est.
english: that, Manlius, is not shameful, rather it is wretched.

latin: ignosces igitur, si, quae mihi luctus ademit,
english: You will pardon, then, if, the ones which grief has taken from me,

latin: haec tibi non tribuo munera, cum nequeo.
english: these gifts I do not bestow on you, since I cannot.

latin: nam quod scriptorum non magna est copia apud me,
english: For that of writings not a great supply is with me,

latin: hoc fit quod Romae vivimus: illa domus,
english: this happens because at Rome we live: that is the home,

latin: illa mihi sedes, illic mea carpitur aetas;
english: that my seat, there my life is plucked away;
note: carpitur: is plucked, i.e. spent.

latin: huc una ex multis capsula me sequitur.
english: hither one out of many little book-boxes follows me.
note: capsula: a box for book rolls.

latin: quod cum ita sit, nolim statuas nos mente maligna
english: Since this is so, I would not wish you to judge that we with a grudging mind

latin: id facere aut animo non satis ingenuo
english: do this or with a spirit not sufficiently generous,

latin: quod tibi non utriusque petenti copia parta est:
english: that to you, asking, not of either a supply has been provided:
note: utriusque: of either gift (of the Muses or of Venus).

latin: ultro ego deferrem, copia si qua foret.
english: unasked I would offer, if there were any supply.

latin: non possum reticere, deae, qua me Allius in re
english: I cannot keep silent, goddesses, in what matter me Allius
note: deae: the Muses. Allius is Merrill's reading of the friend's name (other editors Manlius or Mallius).

latin: iuverit aut quantis iuverit officiis,
english: helped, or with how great services he helped,

latin: ne fugiens saeclis obliviscentibus aetas
english: lest fleeing time, with forgetting generations,
note: saeclis obliviscentibus: ablative absolute, 'as the ages forget'.

latin: illius hoc caeca nocte tegat studium:
english: may cover this zeal of his in blind night:
note: illius ... studium: his devoted service.

latin: sed dicam vobis, vos porro dicite multis
english: but I will tell you, you in turn tell many

latin: milibus et facite haec charta loquatur anus
english: thousands, and make this page speak, an old woman,
note: charta ... anus: anus used as an adjective, 'the paper when grown old', i.e. in ages to come.
A line is lost in the manuscripts here; the gap marker is kept.

latin: notescatque magis mortuus atque magis,
english: and may he become known more, dead, and more,
note: magis ... atque magis: more and more after his death.

latin: nec tenuem texens sublimis aranea telam
english: nor, weaving a thin web, the spider aloft
note: sublimis: aloft, high up (predicative with aranea).

audit.problem: sublimis rendered 'high-hanging', adding 'hanging'; literal is 'aloft/lofty'.

latin: in deserto Alli nomine opus faciat.
english: on the deserted name of Allius do its work.
note: Metaphor: may his name never lie neglected under cobwebs, i.e. be forgotten.

latin: nam mihi quam dederit duplex Amathusia curam
english: For what care to me the twofold Amathusian gave
note: Amathusia: Venus, from Amathus in Cyprus; duplex 'twofold', i.e. deceitful, or giving both joy and pain.

audit.problem: duplex rendered interpretively as 'double-dealing'; literal 'twofold/double', with the deceit sense in the note.

latin: scitis, et in quo me corruerit genere,
english: you know, and in what manner she overthrew me,
note: corruerit: brought me down, ruined me.

latin: cum tantum arderem quantum Trinacria rupes
english: when I burned as much as the Trinacrian rock
note: Trinacria rupes: Etna in Sicily.

latin: lymphaque in Oetaeis Malia Thermopylis,
english: and the Malian water in Oetaean Thermopylae,
note: The hot springs at Thermopylae near Mount Oeta and the Malian gulf.

latin: maesta neque adsiduo tabescere lumina fletu
english: and the sad lights neither from constant weeping to waste away
note: lumina: 'lights', i.e. the poet's eyes. neque ... cessarent: the eyes did not cease to waste away, (and) the cheeks (did not cease) to be wet.

audit.problem: supplied possessive 'my' added without a note. (maesta lumina)

latin: cessarent tristique imbre madere genae,
english: ceased, and with sad rain to be wet the cheeks,
note: imbre: shower, i.e. tears. genae: the poet's cheeks.

audit.problem: supplied possessive 'my' added without a note. (genae)

latin: qualis in aerii perlucens vertice montis
english: such as, shining clear on the top of a lofty mountain,
note: Simile: the stream may illustrate the flowing tears (15-16) or the relief Allius brought (23-26); commentators divide.

latin: rivus muscoso prosilit e lapide,
english: a stream leaps out from a mossy stone,

latin: qui, cum de prone praeceps est valle volutus,
english: which, when headlong down the sloping valley it has rolled,
note: prone: Merrill's spelling for prona, 'sloping'.

latin: per medium densi transit iter populi,
english: crosses through the middle of the road of a dense people,
note: densi populi: crowded with people.

latin: dulce viatori lasso in sudore levamen
english: a sweet relief to the traveller weary in sweat,

audit.problem: supplied possessive 'his' added without a note. (in sudore)

latin: cum gravis exustos aestus hiulcat agros.
english: when heavy heat cracks open the burnt-up fields.

latin: hic, velut in nigro iactatis turbine nautis
english: Here, as to sailors tossed in a black whirlwind

latin: lenius adspirans aura secunda venit
english: breathing more gently a favouring breeze comes,

latin: iam prece Pollucis, iam Castoris implorata,
english: implored now by prayer of Pollux, now of Castor,
note: prece Pollucis ... Castoris: prayer to Pollux and Castor, protectors of sailors.

latin: tale fuit nobis Allius auxilium.
english: such a help to us was Allius.

latin: is clausum lato patefecit limite campum,
english: He opened a closed field with a broad path,
note: Metaphor: he gave access to a love that had been shut off to the poet; limes is a boundary-path.

latin: isque domum nobis isque dedit dominae,
english: and he a house to us, and he gave to a mistress,
note: dominae: to my mistress (Lesbia), or the 'mistress' of the house; disputed.

latin: ad quam communes exerceremus amores.
english: at which we might practise shared loves.
note: quam: feminine, referring to domum (house) of line 28.

audit.problem: supplied possessive 'our' added without a note. (communes amores)

latin: quo mea se molli candida diva pede
english: whither my radiant goddess with soft foot herself
note: candida diva: the beloved (Lesbia).

latin: intulit et trito fulgentem in limine plantam
english: brought, and on the worn threshold the shining sole
note: fulgentem plantam: her (the goddess's) gleaming foot; planta: sole of the foot.

audit.problem: supplied possessive 'her' added without a note. (fulgentem plantam)

latin: innixa arguta constituit solea,
english: resting, set it down with a creaking sandal,
note: arguta solea: sandal that squeaks or clicks; treading on the threshold was an omen.

latin: coniugis ut quondam flagrans advenit amore
english: as once, burning with love of a husband, came
note: coniugis: of her husband (Protesilaus).

audit.problem: supplied possessive 'her' added without a note. (coniugis)

latin: Protesilaeam Laodamia domum
english: to the Protesilaean house Laodamia,
note: Laodamia, bride of Protesilaus, the first Greek killed at Troy.

latin: inceptam frustra, nondum cum sanguine sacro
english: begun in vain, when not yet with sacred blood

latin: hostia caelestis pacificasset eros.
english: a victim had appeased the heavenly masters.
note: eros: accusative plural of erus, 'masters', i.e. the gods; the proper sacrifice before building the house was omitted.

latin: nil mihi tam valde placeat, Rhamnusia virgo,
english: Let nothing please me so greatly, Rhamnusian virgin,
note: Rhamnusia virgo: Nemesis, worshipped at Rhamnus in Attica.

latin: quod temere invitis suscipiatur eris.
english: that it would be undertaken rashly with the masters unwilling.
note: eris: the gods, as in line 36.

latin: quam ieiuna pium desideret ara cruorem
english: how the fasting altar longs for pious blood

latin: docta est amisso Laodamia viro,
english: Laodamia learned, the husband lost,
note: amisso viro: ablative absolute, her husband (Protesilaus) lost.

audit.problem: supplied possessive 'her' added without a note. (amisso viro)

latin: coniugis ante coacta novi dimittere collum
english: forced before to let go the neck of a new husband
note: ante ... quam (41-42): 'before ... than', i.e. before one winter and another had sated her love. coniugis novi: of her new husband.

audit.problem: supplied possessive 'her' added without a note. (coniugis novi)

latin: quam veniens una atque altera rursus hiems
english: than, coming one and another again, winter

latin: noctibus in longis avidum saturasset amorem,
english: in long nights had sated greedy love,
note: avidum amorem: her (Laodamia's) eager love.

audit.problem: supplied possessive 'her' added without a note. (avidum amorem)

latin: posset ut abrupto vivere coniugio:
english: so that she could live with marriage broken off:

latin: quod scibant Parcae non longo tempore abesse,
english: which the Fates knew to be not a long time away,
note: non longo tempore abesse: 'to be not far off' (his death).

latin: si miles muros isset ad Iliacos:
english: if as a soldier he had gone to the Ilian walls:
note: Iliacos: of Ilium, Troy.

latin: nam tum Helenae raptu primores Argivorum
english: for then by the seizure of Helen the foremost of the Argives
note: raptu: abduction, carrying off.

latin: coeperat ad sese Troia ciere viros,
english: Troy had begun to summon to itself, men,
note: primores ... viros (47-48): the foremost men of the Argives.

latin: Troia (nefas) commune sepulcrum Asiae Europaeque,
english: Troy (horror!) the common tomb of Asia and Europe,
note: nefas: unspeakable thing; the parenthesis is in the Latin.

latin: Troia virum et virtutum omnium acerba cinis:
english: Troy the bitter ash of men and of all virtues:
note: virum: genitive plural of vir; cinis here feminine (acerba).

latin: quaene etiam nostro letum miserabile fratri
english: which also to our brother a pitiful death
note: quaene: Merrill's reading, an emphatic relative ('which indeed'); others read quae nunc or quae vetet. nostro: 'our' for 'my'.

latin: attulit. Hei misero frater adempte mihi,
english: brought. Alas, brother taken from wretched me,

latin: hei misero fratri iucundum lumen ademptum,
english: alas, a pleasant light taken from a wretched brother,
note: iucundum lumen: the light of life, or (for the poet) the joy of his life; misero fratri is dative.

latin: tecum una tota est nostra sepulta domus,
english: with you together all our house is buried,

latin: omnia tecum una perierunt gaudia nostra,
english: all with you together have perished our joys,

latin: quae tuus in vita dulcis alebat amor.
english: which your sweet love in life used to nourish.

latin: quem nunc tam longe non inter nota sepulcra
english: whom now so far away not among known tombs

latin: nec prope cognatos compositum cineres,
english: nor laid to rest near kindred ashes,

latin: sed Troia obscena, Troia infelice sepultum
english: but buried in Troy the obscene, Troy the unlucky,
note: obscena: ill-omened, accursed.

latin: detinet extremo terra aliena solo.
english: a foreign land holds back in a farthest soil.
note: extremo solo: at the end of the earth.

latin: ad quam tum properans fertur simul undique pubes
english: to which then, hastening together from everywhere, is said the youth
note: fertur (61) governs deseruisse (62): 'is said to have deserted'.

latin: Graeca penetralis deseruisse focos,
english: Greek, to have deserted the inner hearths,
note: Graeca agrees with pubes (61): the Greek youth. penetralis focos: the hearths of the inner house, i.e. their homes.

audit.problem: supplied possessive 'their' added without a note. (penetralis focos)

latin: ne Paris abducta gavisus libera moecha
english: lest Paris, rejoicing in the carried-off adulteress, free
note: libera agrees with otia (64): 'free leisure'. moecha: adulteress (Helen).

latin: otia pacato degeret in thalamo.
english: leisure should spend in a peaceful bedchamber.

latin: quo tibi tum casu, pulcherrima Laodamia,
english: By which mischance then from you, most beautiful Laodamia,

latin: ereptum est vita dulcius atque anima
english: was snatched, sweeter than life and soul,

latin: coniugium: tanto te absorbens vertice amoris
english: marriage: in so great a whirlpool of love swallowing you
note: coniugium: your (Laodamia's) marriage, subject of ereptum est (66). vertice: whirlpool, eddy.

audit.problem: supplied possessive 'your' added without a note. (coniugium)

latin: aestus in abruptum detulerat barathrum,
english: the surge had carried down into a sheer abyss,
note: Metaphor: her love as a flood sweeping her into an abyss.

latin: quale ferunt Grai Pheneum prope Cylleneum
english: such as the Greeks say near Cyllenean Pheneus

latin: siccare emulsa pingue palude solum,
english: dries, the marsh drained off, the rich soil,
note: siccare: infinitive after ferunt (the Greeks say [it] dries); the drained marsh at Pheneus in Arcadia, below Mount Cyllene.

latin: quod quondam caesis montis fodisse medullis
english: which once, the marrow of the mountain cut, to have dug
note: medullis: marrow, i.e. the heart of the mountain.

latin: audit falsiparens Amphitryoniades,
english: is said the falsely-fathered son of Amphitryon,
note: audit: 'is spoken of as having dug'. falsiparens Amphitryoniades: Hercules, whose putative father Amphitryon was not his true father (Jupiter).

latin: tempore quo certa Stymphalia monstra sagitta
english: at the time when with sure arrow the Stymphalian monsters
note: The Stymphalian birds.

latin: perculit imperio deterioris eri,
english: he struck down at the command of a worse master,
note: deterioris eri: Eurystheus.

latin: pluribus ut caeli tereretur ianua divis,
english: so that by more gods the door of heaven might be worn,
note: Hercules is to be deified, adding to the gods who tread heaven's threshold.

latin: Hebe nec longa virginitate foret.
english: and Hebe not in long virginity might be.
note: Hebe becomes Hercules' wife in heaven.

latin: sed tuus altus amor barathro fuit altior illo,
english: But your deep love was deeper than that abyss,

latin: qui tunc indomitam ferre iugum docuit.
english: which then taught the untamed one to bear the yoke.
note: qui: masculine, = amor. indomitam: feminine, Laodamia. iugum: the yoke of marriage (metaphor).

latin: nam nec tam carum confecto aetate parenti
english: For neither so dear to a parent worn out by age

latin: una caput seri nata nepotis alit,
english: does an only daughter rear the head of a late grandson,
note: caput: head, i.e. the person (the child).

latin: qui, cum divitiis vix tandem inventus avitis
english: who, when, found at last scarcely for the ancestral riches,
note: divitiis avitis: dative, an heir for the grandfather's wealth.

latin: nomen testatas intulit in tabulas,
english: has brought the name into the witnessed tablets,
note: nomen: his own name, entered as heir. testatas tabulas: the attested will.

audit.problem: supplied possessive 'his' added without a note. (nomen)

latin: impia derisi gentilis gaudia tollens
english: taking away the impious joys of the mocked kinsman,
note: gentilis: clansman who hoped to inherit.

latin: suscitat a cano vulturium capiti:
english: rouses the vulture from the grey head:
note: Metaphor: the legacy-hunter (vulture) is driven off from the old man.

latin: nec tantum niveo gavisa est ulla columbo
english: nor so much did any rejoice in a snowy dove
note: columbo: male dove, i.e. her mate; gavisa est (perfect).

audit.problem: supplied possessive 'her' added without a note. (niveo columbo)

latin: compar, quae multo dicitur improbius
english: mate, who is said much more shamelessly

latin: oscula mordenti semper decerpere rostro
english: kisses with biting beak always to pluck

latin: quam quae praecipue multivola est mulier:
english: than she who is especially a much-desiring woman:
note: multivola: wanting many (lovers).

latin: sed tu horum magnos vicisti sola furores,
english: but you alone surpassed the great frenzies of these,
note: horum: masculine/neuter plural genitive, of these (examples).

latin: ut semel es flavo conciliata viro.
english: once you were joined to a golden-haired husband.
note: ut semel: as soon as, once. flavo viro: to your fair-haired man (Protesilaus).

audit.problem: supplied possessive 'your' added without a note. (flavo viro)

latin: aut nihil aut paulo cui tum concedere digna
english: to whom then worthy to yield either nothing or a little
note: cui: dative, Laodamia; the beloved yields to her not at all or only a little.

latin: lux mea se nostrum contulit in gremium,
english: my light betook herself into our lap,
note: lux mea: the beloved (Lesbia). nostrum: 'our' for 'my'.

latin: quam circumcursans hinc illinc saepe Cupido
english: whom, running around this way and that, often Cupid

latin: fulgebat crocina candidus in tunica.
english: shone, bright in a saffron tunic.
note: quam (93) is the object of circumcursans (running around her).

latin: quae tamenetsi uno non est contenta Catullo,
english: who, although with one is not content Catullus,
note: uno ... Catullo: ablative, 'with Catullus alone'.

latin: rara verecundae furta feremus erae,
english: the rare thefts of a modest mistress we will bear,
note: furta: stolen love, infidelities (metaphor). erae: mistress (as of a slave), i.e. the poet's beloved.

audit.problem: supplied possessive 'my' added without a note. (verecundae erae)

latin: ne nimium simus stultorum more molesti:
english: lest we be too troublesome in the manner of fools:

latin: saepe etiam Iuno, maxima caelicolum,
english: often even Juno, greatest of the heaven-dwellers,

latin: coniugis in culpa flagrantem concoquit iram
english: at a husband's fault digests blazing wrath,
note: concoquit: digests (metaphor), i.e. swallows, suppresses her anger. coniugis: of her husband (Jupiter).

audit.problem: supplied possessives 'her' twice (coniugis, iram) added without a note.

latin: noscens omnivoli plurima furta Iovis.
english: knowing the very many thefts of all-desiring Jove.
note: furta: stolen loves (metaphor).

latin: atqui nec divis homines componier aequum est

english: than as mother to bear brothers from an uncle.
note: fratres ex patruo: children by her uncle, who are her sons and cousins at once.

latin: Multus homo est, Naso, neque tecum multus homo est qui
english: Much of a man he is, Naso, and not with you much of a man is he who
note: multus homo: 'much of a man', a pun on many-sided/great man; the sense of the couplet is obscure.

latin: descendit: Naso, multus es et pathicus.
english: goes down: Naso, you are much, and a pathic.
note: descendit: goes down (to the forum, or in a sexual sense). pathicus: the passive partner in anal sex.

latin: Consule Pompeio primum duo, Cinna, solebant
english: With Pompey consul the first time, two, Cinna, used to have
note: Verb not expressed in the Latin; 'have' supplied from the sexual sense. solebant: 'used to'.

latin: Maeciliam: facto consule nunc iterum
english: Maecilia: now, with him made consul again,

latin: manserunt duo, sed creverunt milia in unum
english: the two have remained, but there have grown thousands for one

latin: singula. fecundum semen adulterio.
english: each. Fertile seed in adultery.
note: singula: each (lover) has become thousands.

latin: Firmanus saltu non falso Mentula dives
english: Firmanian, with his estate, not falsely, Mentula rich
note: Firmanus saltu: by his estate at Firmum.

latin: fertur, qui tot res in se habet egregias,
english: is said to be, which has in itself so many outstanding things,
note: qui: masculine, referring to saltus (the estate, line 1); in se: in itself (the estate).

audit.problem: qui with reflexive in se must refer to the estate (saltus), as the writer's own note says, so 'who ... in it' wrongly makes Mentula the antecedent and breaks the reflexive.

latin: aucupium omne genus, piscis, prata, arva, ferasque.
english: fowling of every kind, fish, meadows, ploughland, and wild beasts.

latin: nequiquam: fructus sumptibus exsuperat.
english: In vain: he exceeds the yield by expenses.
note: fructus: accusative plural, the yield; sumptibus: by (his) expenses, i.e. he spends more than the estate produces.

audit.problem: Possessive 'his' (expenses) supplied without a note.

latin: quare concedo sit dives, dum omnia desint;
english: Therefore I grant he be rich, provided all things be lacking;
note: sit, desint: subjunctives; concedo sit: I grant (that) he be.

audit.problem: sit is subjunctive (concessive 'let him be rich'); 'he is rich' flattens the mood.

latin: saltum laudemus, dum domo ipse egeat.
english: let us praise the estate, provided he himself is in need at home.

latin: Mentula habet iuxta triginta iugera prati,
english: Mentula has nearly thirty jugera of meadow,
note: iuxta: nearly; iugera: acres (iugera).

latin: quadraginta arvi: cetera sunt maria.
english: forty of ploughland: the rest are seas.

latin: cur non divitiis Croesum superare potis sit
english: Why not in riches Croesus could he surpass,

latin: uno qui in saltu tot bona possideat,
english: he who in one estate possesses so many goods,

latin: prata, arva, ingentis silvas saltusque paludesque
english: meadows, ploughlands, huge woods and woodland-pastures and marshes

latin: usque ad Hyperboreos et mare ad Oceanum?
english: as far as the Hyperboreans and the sea to Ocean?

latin: omnia magna haec sunt, tamen ipse est maximus ultro,
english: All these are great, yet he himself is greatest beyond them,

latin: non homo, sed vero mentula magna minax.
english: not a man, but truly a prick, great, threatening.
note: mentula: 'prick', pun on the nickname Mentula.

latin: Saepe tibi studioso animo venante requirens
english: Often for you, with a studious mind hunting, seeking
note: animo venante: ablative, with the mind hunting.

latin: carmina uti possem mittere Battiadae
english: how I might be able to send songs of Battiades
note: Battiadae: Callimachus, son of Battus.

latin: qui te lenirem nobis, neu conarere
english: by which I might soften you to us, and that you would not try

latin: tela infesta mihi mittere in usque caput,
english: hostile weapons to send at me even up to the head,
note: Metaphor kept: weapons = abusive verses. caput: (my) head.

audit.problem: Possessive 'my' (head) supplied without a note.

latin: hunc video mihi nunc frustra sumptum esse laborem,
english: this I see now for me in vain has been undertaken, labour,

latin: Gelli, nec nostras hic valuisse preces.
english: Gellius, and our prayers here not to have prevailed.

latin: contra nos tela ista tua evitamus amictu:
english: In turn we avoid those weapons of yours with a cloak:
note: contra: adverb, in turn, on the other hand (some take contra nos 'against us'); nos: we (= I). amictu: cloak, wrapped garment; i.e. I will parry your verses.

audit.problem: contra is adverbial ('in turn', as the writer's own note says) and nos is the subject; 'Against them' adds 'them' and turns contra into a preposition.

latin: at fixus nostris tu dabis supplicium.
english: but pierced by ours you will pay the penalty.
note: nostris: by our (weapons).
